Gen X here. I grew up in an era of eye-rolling and pearl-clutching about how much we were overmedicating children. I have finally been diagnosed with ADHD and OCD after wasting years of my time and thousands of dollars on pharmaceutical and behavioral therapy for anxiety and depression that never really helped me “all the way.” 

The last psychiatrist I saw blew me off when I told her that I thought I had OCD. I concluded that my brain was broken in a way that couldn’t be fixed and gave up on ever feeling happy again. Then my young son was diagnosed with OCD and I went back and asked her to re-evaluate me. I finally got referred to a therapist specializing in OCD and feel hopeful for the first time in years. 

My therapist is the one who noticed that I also had ADHD symptoms. I initially scoffed at the idea—until she told me what the symptoms were. She said ADHD is underdiagnosed in girls and young women because they are able to mask it more effectively than boys, but that many women’s symptoms become acutely worse during menopause.

It’s appalling that I had to suffer major losses of function personally and professionally and ultimately  diagnose myself before I could get effective help from any of the mental health professionals I saw over the years. I don’t blame young women for taking matters into their own hands for a single second.

Increasingly, Chinese goods are routed through Canada (or Mexico), where Canadian firms perform limited assembly, and export finished goods to the U.S. under preferential terms.  The goods are improperly claimed as USMCA-eligible or Canadian-origin, circumventing the China-specific duty. 

The total value of transshipped goods -- including kitchen cabinets, trailer parts, many steel-related products -- may be as high as $303 billion a year, and growing.  Transshipment without “substantial transformation” is illegal under customs rules.

 Under Prime Minister Mark Carney, the illegal circumvention is semi-official Canadian policy.  

Canada struck a "strategic partnership" with China that reduced the EV tariff to the most-favored-nation rate of 6.1% for a quota of up to 49,000 vehicles annually (with expectations of related Chinese investment in Canada’s auto sector). Just 7% of America’s Nuclear Fuel Comes From Home93% of the uranium used in US nuclear fuel comes from foreign sources, with critical enrichment supply chains concentrated among a small number of countries, including Russia.

Global uranium demand is projected to rise 28% by 2030 and nearly double by 2040, and US utilities already face a 186 million pound gap between projected demand and existing long-term contracts.

The US is racing to close the gap through spent-fuel recycling, a major new in-situ recovery site in South Texas, and talks to convert Cold War-era weapons-grade plutonium into commercial reactor fuel.

At present, a whopping 93 percent of the United States’ uranium for nuclear fuel is coming from foreign markets. Uranium production and enrichment are overwhelmingly carried out by a worryingly small number of players, and many of these critical supply chains are controlled by Russia. These articles drive me a bit crazy. I grew up in Los Altos, my office is currently less than two miles from the Waldorf school mentioned here, and I’ve spent 25 years working with teens in Silicon Valley. I’ve written four books, including Social Media Wellness, and in 2018 I wrote “The Secret Social Media Lives of Teenagers” for this paper. I’ve been in the trenches on this issue for a long time.

Nearly all the parents interviewed for this piece (and pieces like it!) have young children, not teenagers or young adults. It’s easy to restrict a five- or seven-year-old. Talk to me when your kids are 15 and 17.

Tech executives with teenagers and young adults grapple with exactly the same issues around gaming, YouTube, and social media that every other parent does. I’ve worked with many families in this exact position — including prominent CEOs, tech execs and VCs — whose kids were spending hours every day/night on YouTube, gaming, TikTok and/or Instagram, and it took concentrated and intentional efforts to make long term behavioral changes.

Helping kids and teens make good decisions online and off is hard. comments.body:
Everything has fallen apart for most of us. When I was a kid in the 80s and 90s there was a social fabric and it had many layers.

I remember waking up in my small town to the smell and sounds of the Lions Club and its older male members sitting in woven lawn chairs flipping pancakes, smoking cigarettes, and drinking coffee. They’d serve up breakfast to anyone who walked up. There was the grange hall and its members. Churches of all types. So many community organizations to join and network within and find your place in one or several layers of the social fabric that makes up a place. 

If I skipped school in my town and any adult saw me walking around town they’d pop the passenger door open and tell me to get in, they’re taking me back to school or home, and then say they were calling my mom. I know this sounds endearing and also kind of overbearing, but that’s social fabric. People have to feel like they belong, so much so that they’re willing to roll the dice and risk caring too much.

My husband and I talk about how these social groups are dying. There’s no old guard or network of adults passing on the torch to burgeoning adults. But young people don’t want kids or marriage. 

Everyone it seems has soured on anything that requires giving up your free time and being selfless. 

We don’t have to live like this. Volunteer, find a church, join a book club, or anything involving other people and invest your time in them. Good things will grow.

Demonstrating commonalities is a path to becoming friends.  It doesn't even have to be structured.  In college in the 80s, people became friends because they were in the TV lounge to watch the same show every week.  Today, that might be equivalent to being at a sports bar, or sitting in the same seat at the local high school football game every week. My biological father passed away from cancer in 1997, never knowing that I, and several other of his offspring, existed. It was neat to learn that he was 100% Italian, Sicilian to be exact. 23andMe even knew what city in Sicily the family roots could be found, Carlentini. I confirmed this through Ancestry.com and was amazed that 23andMe could figure that out from my genetics. 

My biological father gave me some great genes, I have a full head of hair at 67! When I saw his photo, I could see myself in him. I had a photo of him standing by his tent during the Korean War, and my own son thought the photo was of me!

But, I soon realized that shared genetics doesn't a family make. I never connected with my half-siblings beyond a superficial exchange of background info. It just wasn't meant to be - I no longer keep in touch with them. That's okay.

It's important, and really nice to know, that it often does work out and families are found and founded. I'm glad Ms. Moses shared this story.

The great thing about the Valley is we're just a hop away from all the exciting features on the other side of "the hill" but when we're done there, we can go home to our quiet neighborhoods.

comments.name: lagreyeyes
comments.body:
I remember when the 213 area code stretched all the way through Westlake Village, where I grew up, to the Ventura County border. We definitely didn’t enjoy the sudden change to 818 and its association with the Valley.

Yes, just like those in “the city” (Los Angeles), we used to be condescending to the SFV. “Our beach!”, from original Malibu through Zuma, was our rallying teenage cry toward the provincial interlopers each summer. But after I moved out of my folks’ house into a Woodland Hills apartment, my attitude changed. So much to do! Movie theaters! Malls! So many restaurants on Ventura Blvd! Lots of fun and I really enjoyed the few years I lived there. Heckuva lot more exciting than WLV! Both the city proper and the SVF have their good and bad pockets, like all places.

(But never tell the now-snooty denizens of Calabasas that they’re actually part of the Valley. Everything over the Calabasas grade is. Yet they’ll ALWAYS deny it, lol.)

Long live the San Fernando Valley!

comments.name: Giveret Davar
comments.body: Not mentioned in the article or by any of my fellow Boomer Valley denizens was how lovely, peaceful & quiet the Valley was when we were growing up in the 50's & 60's.  Large swaths of the Valley were still farmland.  In the spring, the air was redolent with the perfume of the multitude of orange gloves, now sadly gone.  Some neighborhoods still boasted old farmhouses that gave the neighborhoods charm--much more charm than some of the mausoleum-type monstrosities seen now.  Things have advanced in many good ways since then, thanks to the civil rights movement, the women's movement, LGBT rights, etc.  But I sure miss those Orange groves whenever I come back to visit.

I'm not opposed to surrogacy, but people considering it assume significant risks. There's a reason that only the rich can afford surrogacy - you need expensive legal services on both sides to ensure parental rights are assigned/terminated correctly, but there are always potential pitfalls. We shouldn't ban surrogacy, but more regulation is required to prevent bad actors from exploiting people.

I'm glad the ADF is defending this woman. To force a young woman to have an abortion is cruel; the thought of putting that type of provision in a contract casts serious doubt on both the couple's morality and the quality of their legal representation. I do think, however, that the couple is entitled to custody. I doubt a judge would strike the whole agreement just because of one unenforceable provision. But it's a little rich to seek custody after requesting that the baby's life be ended.

comments.name: Jonathan
comments.body:
The columnist is omitting a lot of facts. First, the heart defect is not a death sentence. The medical professionals explained that without treatment the child would likely die. They were told that multiple surgeries would be required but there were many cases where post-operative results are positive. Some who have had similar surgeries as infants are now in their 40s. 

The other consideration omitted is that the surrogate exercised her rights as the gestational "mother" to choose to proceed with the pregnancy. Her body, her decision. What is called a pro-choice position.

comments.name: Betsy
comments.body: Pregnancy works most of the time, and then it doesn’t. This is a tragic case on all levels. Take care of the baby while all these other issues are resolved. Time to rethink the surrogacy industry.

comments.name: JerseyGirl

We're told that abortion is "a women's choice" -- except when that woman is legally bound to abort the child growing in her womb under the terms of a commercial contract.

Commercial surrogacy is illegal in all western countries except the US.  It is a moral and legal abomination and should be  prohibited in the US.

comments.name: Ravnwing
comments.body:
There are no guarantees when it comes to childbirth. You can do everything right and plan for every possible outcome and things can still go very wrong. Surrogacy just adds another layer of complication into the mix because you are dealing with the woman carrying the wanted fetus (and is being financially compensated to do so) and the parents (genetic or otherwise) who wish to raise the baby when it is born and are paying a large amount of money. It is bound to happen that sooner or later, those interests are going to go into conflict. Even if they start out on the same page when the contracts are signed, things can change over the course of the pregnancy.

It is clear that the gestational surrogate violated the contract and the fled across state lines to a state that would be friendlier to her argument. Regardless of what she might have thought the parents would really wish if the worst happened, she signed a contract agreeing to terminate under these circumstances. She is responsible for understanding what she is agreeing to (and as a nurse, should be able to understand that the contract is legally binding).  She has no rights to the child that was born legally, and per all precedent, his parents should be allowed to take custody and leave Texas as soon as he is medically stable enough to do so.

comments.name: Actuary
comments.body:
Actuaries call this "third-party litigation financing." Essentially, claimants are sought out and extraordinary rewards are pursued. Remember that there are no free lunches, so in order to protect all insureds and follow our principles of ratemaking, we end up having to raise all prices to address the rising costs. 

Insurers must adequately support making legitimate claimants whole. The problem is that a substantial amount of the cost is being taken by lawyers, their investors, and social inflation. We all bear the cost of that through higher premiums and less coverage.

More on TLPF: https://ar.casact.org/financing-justice-the-rise-and-risks-of-tplf/

CAS Principles of Ratemaking: https://www.casact.org/statement-principles-regarding-property-and-casualty-insurance-ratemaking

The United States and Russia were both arming (different) Ukrainians in this civil war, so it was also soon a proxy war. 14,000 Ukrainians were already killed in it prior to Russia's 2022  invasion and cluster bombs were being used by the two sides to maim  one another. Wouldn't a  compromise settlement and long term peace framework be the best possible way to "support the Ukrainians" at this point? Brother against brother and mother against son civil wars only become worse with no real "winners" morally or practically. comments.name: Aishwarya Mohan Gahrana
comments.body:
Private Education in India has not only become a debt trap but has also failed to provide an employable education. These education businesses focus on image-building rather than on building educational infrastructure. Even in primary education, private schools advertise Air Conditioners, swimming pools (not for swimming classes but for pool parties), car parking, etc. They have lavish halls for parents and teachers but an unequipped library and laboratory. 

In recent years, Indian students are getting more marks than earlier generations, but increasingly become unemployable!! 

Most private schools and universities are promoted or developed by political persons. Even if they are not politician at the beginning, parties value them for their influence over captive young voters in their educational captivity. These students are regularly asked to join their political masters' programs and vote for them.

Recently, I referred a law graduate from one of the universities named in this article to a decent law firm; she was rejected even before the interview started. This feeling is across courses.

Businesses say these "purchased" degrees are not of use to us. This is a sorry state of affairs for students, who are paying for education, not for a degree. 

We need an overhaul - from class 1 to the last. 

I am waiting for a follow-up story from the industry on why they mistrust students of these private institutes.

comments.name: Former Tea Party big player
comments.body: India's leaders have failed the people. Corrupt to the core. It is time  that its people change the leadership, thoroughly and hold them accountable. The majority young should prevail.  Anything else is a slow grind to mindlessness.

comments.name: Anonymous Human
comments.body: Fantastic news coverage as usual by the excellent Alex Travelli, and the NYT team in India. As someone who grew up in India in the 70s and 80s, I did well in the Indian education system till about high school, when I decided I had enough of memorizing enormous amounts of information for regurgitation on tests. I ended up moving into the US higher education system, where I could actually have a proper conversation with the professor, and we could debate things. Best of all, at work people cared that I solved real world problems, and if I solved a few, they gave me more. I tell people I failed in India, and succeeded in the US. If your focus is on practical problem-solving, you will do fine, with or without education, anywhere in the world. Education is about providing context, but you still have to have the tenacity and drive to help the world, and make a real impact, not just an impression. I feel for these students. However, the world is much different today than when I grew up. So many kids in India have a shot at being creative, and have so many different technology tools and business models at their disposal. They should not put themselves in a prison of their own making, whereby they think that education is going to be their ticket to the future. Education is good, but applying yourself is even better. Indian culture can trap people in thinking that education and status are what make a person. Self-discovery and self-definition are equally important.

The cost of education in these establishments doesn't reflect the quality of education imparted, but rather how much students are willing to pay to get a degree. comments.name: c.c.
comments.body: Thank you for this article, good to know there's a new med to try.  As a kid I loved rollercoasters and swings and was even a gymnast twisting and spinning with no problems, but as an adult I get motion sickness doing these activities.  I have had the most success preventing motion sickness with a scopolamine patch but I hate the dry mouth.  In extremely rough seas The Relief Band has helped as well.  I thought it strange that once on land if I turned off the Relief Band I immediately felt sick, turned it back on and I was fine.  I needed to keep the band on for a day or two before I was able to turn it off without the nausea returning.  I have also experienced Mal de Embarquement.  My solution is to leave the scopolamine patch on past its effective date for a few days after a cruise and so far no recurrence of sickness.  How horrible that some people find no relief from Mal de embarquement!

comments.name: Doctor G
comments.body:
In my professional life I've prescribed a lot of scopolamine  for motion sickness and zofran for nausea.  Many people also use OTC Dramamine or Dramamine less drowsy.
They are all usually helpful, and they all sometimes have side effects.  Test them out at home before use on a vacation.
Motion sickness is related to the vestibular system, which is poorly understood.  The inner ear and eyes are involved, but undoubtedly there are complex pathways within the nervous system.  It is probably a multifactorial problem, and no single stimulus will always cause symptoms, nor will one treatment work for everyone.

comments.name: lambjams
comments.body: There are four different types of histamine receptors currently known. Although the different types have different functions, like the H2 receptor is predominantly in the stomach, affecting digestion and stomach acid, there is some overlap and likely genetic variation. I have discovered that one antihistamine for allergies doesn't really work for my motion sickness. However, one targeting H2 receptors, which is supposed to be primarily stomach, affected my sinuses more than expected. I haven't had a chance to test it for motion sickness, but it's worth trying. Neither of these specific antihistamines induced drowsiness, but some of the older antihistamines did.

comments.name: Betsy Y.
comments.body: I find it interesting that an article on motion sickness doesn't include any references to the inner ear and the role of congestion. Motion bands have helped in many situations. I've had multiple instances of vertigo in my life and ear aches. I also had nasal surgery several years ago...I experience less motion sickness now.

comments.name: smith
comments.body: Premier Zhu was the architecture of China's current economic model, an export-oriented model that depresses domestic consumption.  Under Zhu, numerous China's state owned enterprises (SOE) went bankrupt or otherwise reorganized.  Millions of SOE employees suddenly lost their jobs, and many families struggled. He is the person who took back the tax revenue from local government, so that the central government had the resources to invest in areas it prioritized, leading to China's dominance and eventual overcapacities in key industries.  Let's not cancel this part of the history.  President Xi essentially follows the same economic model Premier Zhu established.  The main difference is that China has since moved up the manufactural and technological value chain. The industries it focuses on are no longer the ones we want to source, but the advanced ones that we die to keep and dominate.  What's happening in China's economy is a natural evolution of what Premier Zhu had envisioned and implemented.  His model makes clearcut the effect of government policies on winners and losers.  Our politicians tend to refrain from dramatic policy changes.  But we end up with same number of losers of economic changes.  It's just our losers don't really know who to blame.

Despite all their progress, under the surface and deep down to the core, China is nothing but a House of Cards.  And the Beijing mandarins know it well.

comments.name: Peter
comments.body: While we may not have a modern day economic architect today as brilliant as Premier Zhu,  who stood out with a character resembling Premier Zhou,  empirically I would venture to say many more Chinese have been lifted out of poverty today , many more have better housing, many families have 2 cars,  few are hungry anymore,   such tangible economic gains belied Chinese naysayers in the West. Just like the US, the Chinese economy has its cycles.  In fact, Chinese has more freedom of expression than previous times.  As they often say, it is not an easy task to feed and clothe 1.3 billion people, nor to manage them.  So I think Xi is doing a decent job !

comments.name: Jim
comments.body: Mr. Zhu was considered a reformer at the time and indeed was a force in pushing China toward capitalism. In 1997, I went with GM CEO Jack Smith to China to try to complete a deal that would result in Buick being the first American auto manufacturer in the country. That became the crown plant in GM’s system, the Shanghai auto plant. Interestingly, when we got on the plane for Beijing, we did not have a deal but we had faith that Mr. Zhu would help us get it over the line. At the same time, Vice President Al Gore was also in China trying to get us, Boeing and a few other big American companies access to the market but was shadowed by Chinagate, a foreign fundraising allegation. For days, we ran around in circles but nothing happened until the men at the top said so — and then everything happened. Al Gore and Li Peng toasted the deals in the Great Hall of the People’s and Jack Smith gave a global press conference with about 100 journalists in attendance.

Love your point about the deliberateness that hand-writing adds: the sweet rigor of revision. 

I think you may understate the power of thinking-by-talking: it's good for a lot more than brainstorming (braindumping?) when you've got your hands full.  

This past week, I've been working with my oldest son (21) on a research paper and my youngest (14) on a reflective essay...and, for both (as for many of the students in courses I've taught), talking gives them a way to "get their thinking out" without tangling themselves up in the need to "get it right" that many of us feel when we step onto the writing state. 

Thanks for the piece!

comments.name: Ed

"Writing is a rigorous process to understand your own thoughts and then lay those thoughts out in a way that convinces or inspires or moves other people. But speaking is not that process."

Henry James dictated all of his later work to a secretary while walking around his study, including The Turn of the Screw, The Wings of the Dove, The Ambassadors and the Golden Bowl. Is The Wings of the Dove equivalent to "a quick brainstorm"? It's very funny to me when people's reflexive hatred of technology compels them invent completely new rules for what is or isn't real art, real writing, real work etc. that inadvertently exclude huge swathes of the canon that we used to measure these things against.

It's true that my phone's dictation software needs plenty of proofreading and correction. I owned an oceanfront condo in South Beach and was an HOA board member.  The article is spot-on.  Deferred maintenance created the delusion of affordability while allowing the building to deteriorate for years/decades (building certifications were required every 40 years!).  Any attempt to increase fees for a maintenance/repair fund were met with fierce resistance.  The idea was to pass the bill on to the next owner.  And yes, the infighting was terrible, reminding me of the "sunny place for shady people " character of these paradise-type places.
To be fair, the article misses an important point:  corrupt HOAs and/or management companies (which some buildings hire) are said to be the rule rather than the exception in SoFl. Prices are inflated to cover kickbacks from contractors, jobs are embellished.  Or money just simply disappears.  I didn't see this myself, but it was stated as fact.  So owners have good reason to be suspicious and reluctant to part with their $.
Given the above, the worsening heat that even lifelong residents now complain about,  the frequent beach closures due to fecal contamination, the seaweed tides, the crowds and traffic congestion, my advice is stay away.  If you're already there,  start making your get-away plan.  It's the proverbial nice place to visit but you wouldn't want to live there. It's paradise lost.

comments.name: Rahqeed
comments.body: This is outstanding reporting. One note regarding the new regulations (milestone, SIRS): The mandates are explicitly limited to buildings that are three or more habitable stories in height, the operative word being habitable. Although relatively few, there are buildings throughout Miami Beach that have the ground level floor reserved for parking. While it may seem like splitting hairs, those seeking to buy in the area may opt to focus on well-managed, well maintained smaller buildings with healthy financials and robust reserves that are only two habitable stories and therefore exempt from the new regs. With parking at a premium and king tide (among other climate) threat potential, an ideal option may be a three story building with parking at the ground level. There is a robust supply at the moment at comparatively affordable prices compared to the unsustainable exponential increases in the broader south Florida market and the well-informed buyer working with a local real estate sales expert can find some excellent options at the moment. Ownership costs, especially maddeningly high property taxes and historically high common charges due to insurance premiums, are certainly a factor, but Miami Beach is a vibrant city, a cultural mecca, a destination for culinary excellence, and absolutely gorgeous. With the Atlantic never more than a few minutes walk from anywhere in the city.

They build it, sell it and dissolve the corporation that built.  Liability should for how a high rise building holds up over time should follow them.  If it did they might build with an eye to the future.  Otherwise this problem will only grow overtime. Political leadership is also non-existent.

Then, if the owners decide they don't want to pay to maintain their own home, even at the risk of injury or death, then leave them alone in their stupidity. They only mandatory charge should be a monthly charge to be escrowed for clearing the rubble and recovering bodies should a collapse occur. And if a collapse does occur, the land reverts to the state and nothing may be rebuilt there. After that, everybody should be happy.

Many condo and co-op buildings have kept monthly charges artificially low by underfunding reserves and postponing major repairs. New York may face an even larger problem because much of its housing stock is older. Roofs, façades, elevators, boilers, plumbing, electrical systems, structural repairs, insurance, and energy requirements are imposing costs at once.
Low monthly charges can create a false sense of affordability. A building with inadequate reserves is simply shifting today’s expenses onto tomorrow’s owners who will face crushing special assessments.
The problem extends beyond private housing. New York’s public housing system offers a glaring example of what happens when maintenance and capital replacement are deferred. Residents live with deteriorating conditions because essential repairs were deferred year after year, allowing manageable maintenance needs to become enormous capital liabilities.
New York should require long-term reserve studies for co-ops and condos, fuller disclosure of expected capital needs, and realistic funding plans, while providing targeted assistance to cash-poor homeowners.
The lesson is simple: deferred maintenance eventually comes due. Whether in a luxury condominium or a public housing project, someone has to pay.
